Solid State Physics · Properties of Solids

Module IV — Magnetic & dielectric properties

Theory notes: concepts, results and what every symbol means

Types of magnetism

in one lineEvery solid is magnetic in some way. What kind depends on whether its atoms have permanent moments (unpaired electrons) and on how neighbouring moments line up: not at all, randomly, parallel, antiparallel and equal, antiparallel and unequal.

Magnetic terminology

Put a solid in a magnetic field and it becomes magnetised: tiny current loops inside it line up, or are created, and add their own field. Three quantities describe this. The applied field strength (A/m) is set by the coils outside. The magnetisation (also A/m) is the magnetic moment per unit volume the solid develops. The flux density (tesla) is the total, field plus material. The susceptibility measures how strongly the solid responds:

wheremagnetic susceptibility (no units)magnetisation: magnetic moment per unit volumemagnetising field

In SI, and are both in A/m, so is dimensionless (in general a tensor; a scalar for isotropic media). Per gram-molecule it is the molar susceptibility .

Where an atomic moment comes from

Moving charges are currents, and a current loop is a magnet. An atom has three sources of moment:

  • Orbital motion of the electrons: an electron going round a nucleus is a tiny loop current, with moment .
  • Spin of the electrons: with , so one spin- electron carries about one Bohr magneton.
  • Nuclear spin: smaller by about , ignored here.

Filled shells cancel in pairs (every spin up has a partner down, every orbit has a counter-rotating twin), so the moment of an atom comes from its unpaired electrons. The natural unit is the Bohr magneton,

whereBohr magneton, the natural unit of atomic magnetic momentelectron chargereduced Planck constantelectron mass

Fe has four unpaired 3d electrons, five, so their moments are a few . Atoms with only closed shells (inert gases, , ) have none.

Diamagnetism is present in every material; it is just usually swamped. A substance is called diamagnetic only when it has no permanent moments.

Dia- & paramagnetism

in one lineDiamagnetism: a field speeds up or slows down each electron orbit by the Larmor frequency ; the extra current opposes . Paramagnetism: permanent moments turn towards against thermal disorder; the Boltzmann average gives the Langevin function and the Curie law .

Diamagnetism

When the flux through an orbit changes, an induced current opposes the change (Lenz's law). Switch on a field and every electron orbit is gently sped up or slowed down, in whichever sense makes a moment against the field. The magnetic field of that induced current is opposite to the applied field: a small, negative . It exists in all materials, because every atom has orbiting electrons.

The Larmor picture. The orbit as a whole precesses about at the Larmor frequency . Each electron then carries an extra current , and its loop area is set by the mean square distance from the field axis, for a spherical atom. That is where the and the 6 in the result come from:

Paramagnetism

Now give every atom a permanent moment . Without a field they point at random and cancel. A field tries to line them up (energy ), heat tries to scramble them (). The outcome of that contest is the Boltzmann average of . Paramagnetism is seen in:

  • metals (conduction electrons);
  • atoms and molecules with an odd number of electrons (free Na atoms, NO gas);
  • a few with an even number ();
  • atoms and ions with a partly filled inner shell: rare earths, actinides, transition-metal ions such as .

Ferromagnetism

in one lineWeiss: an internal field proportional to lines the moments up. It explains spontaneous magnetisation below and the Curie–Weiss law above it. The field is the quantum exchange interaction. A lump of iron can be unmagnetised because it is split into domains; moving and turning them gives the hysteresis loop.

Ferromagnetism

Permanent moments, as in paramagnets, but neighbours line up parallel even without a field: spontaneous magnetisation, below the Curie temperature . Above thermal agitation wins and the material is paramagnetic. Large, positive, field-dependent ; magnetisation against field traces a hysteresis curve. Examples: Fe ( K), Ni (631 K), Co (1388 K), Gd (292 K), Dy; alloys and oxides such as MnBi, MnAs, .

Two puzzles need explaining. Why do the moments line up at all, when a paramagnet needs an enormous field to do the same? And if iron is spontaneously magnetised, why is an ordinary iron nail not a magnet? Weiss answered both with two hypotheses.

Weiss theory

Two hypotheses: (i) the specimen is made of small spontaneously magnetised domains, whose moments add as vectors; (ii) inside a domain an exchange (molecular) field lines the moments up, the Weiss constant (independent of ). For iron T.

Above : treat the material as a paramagnet that feels instead of . Solving for gives the Curie–Weiss law:

Origin of the Weiss field: exchange

A dipole–dipole field is about G (0.1 T), far too weak: iron needs about G. Heisenberg (1928): the field comes from the quantum exchange interaction, a consequence of the Pauli principle. Turning one spin changes the allowed spatial wavefunction and so the charge distribution: the energy is electrostatic, not magnetic. The energy of two atoms contains

whereexchange energy of a pair of neighbouring atomsexchange integral ( favours parallel spins)spin vectors of the two atoms

, the exchange integral, depends on the overlap of the two atoms' charge clouds. : parallel spins have lower energy (ferromagnetism). : antiparallel (antiferromagnetism). Bethe–Slater: when (atomic separation ÷ radius of the 3d shell) is a little above 3: Fe, Co, Ni, Gd are ferromagnetic; Mn and Cr are not. Summing over nearest neighbours (Stoner) gives with .

Domains and hysteresis

Why iron is usually unmagnetised: each domain is fully magnetised but the domains point in different directions. Néel: the domain pattern minimises the total energy: exchange, magnetic field energy, anisotropy energy, wall energy and magnetostrictive energy. One big domain has a large external field; splitting lowers that, but every wall costs energy, so the split stops at a balance.

Two processes magnetise a specimen: (a) growth of favourably oriented domains (wall movement) and (b) rotation of domain magnetisation towards the field. They map onto the magnetisation curve:

  • OA (small fields): reversible wall movement.
  • AB: large, irreversible wall movements; rises steeply.
  • BC: domains rotate from their easy directions to the field; creeps up to saturation .
  • Reduce the field: does not retrace the curve. At the remanence is left. The reverse field that removes it is the coercivity . The closed loop is the hysteresis loop; its area is the energy lost per cycle.

Soft materials (small , thin loop: transformer cores, electromagnets; soft iron, Si-steel) and hard materials (large and : permanent magnets; alnico, ferrite magnets).

Antiferro & ferri

in one lineNegative exchange makes neighbours antiparallel. Two equal sublattices cancel (antiferromagnetism: small with a cusp at the Néel temperature). Two unequal ones leave a net moment (ferrimagnetism: ferrite, magnetite), which behaves outwardly like a ferromagnet.

Antiferromagnetism

Spins of neighbouring atoms antiparallel (exchange integral negative). Think of two interpenetrating sublattices A and B, magnetised in opposite directions: no net magnetisation. First seen in MnO ( K); also FeO, NiO, CoO, , Cr. A field gives a small magnetisation that increases with temperature up to the Néel temperature , then falls (paramagnetic). At , is not infinite but has a weak cusp.

Néel's theory above . Each sublattice is a paramagnet that feels the applied field minus molecular fields from the other sublattice () and from its own (). The minus signs are the whole story: the neighbours fight the field instead of helping it.

Ferrimagnetism

The same antiparallel arrangement, but the sublattice magnetisations are unequal, so a net magnetisation survives. Found in ferrites, double oxides of the form (M = Mn, Co, Ni, Cu, Mg, Zn, Fe) with the spinel structure: oxygen ions in a close-packed cubic array, metal ions in the gaps between them. Two kinds of gap: A (tetrahedral) sites with four neighbours and B (octahedral) sites with six. The A–B exchange is strongly negative, so the A and B sublattices point opposite ways.

Magnetite = : one on an A site; one and the on B sites. The two moments (5 each, ) cancel, and the net moment per formula unit is that of one , 4 (: four unpaired electrons). Experiment gives 4.1 . A spinel unit cell holds 8 formula units.

learn this by heart

Ferrimagnet in one line: antiparallel and unequal sublattices. Net moment = difference of the sublattice moments. Outwardly like a ferromagnet (spontaneous , Curie point, domains, hysteresis), but with a much smaller saturation moment and a very high electrical resistivity.

Above the Curie temperature both sublattices follow Curie–Weiss-like laws and is a hyperbola rather than a straight line; below it, saturation sets in. Ferrites are ceramics with resistivities up to times that of iron, so eddy-current losses are tiny: the standard cores for high-frequency transformers, inductors, antenna rods and microwave devices.

, local field, C–M

in one lineA field pulls the bound charges of a dielectric slightly apart: polarisation . An atom feels not the average field but the local field . Putting that into gives the Clausius–Mossotti relation between and .

Polarisation and susceptibility

Dielectrics are insulators: no free carriers, so no current flows. But their bound positive and negative charges can shift by a fraction of an atomic diameter in a field. Each atom or molecule becomes a small dipole (charge separation), and the polarisation is the dipole moment per unit volume. The bound charges that appear on the surfaces make a polarisation field opposing the applied field:

wherefield inside the dielectricapplied fieldfield of the polarisation charges (it opposes )polarisation: dipole moment per unit volumepermittivity of free spaceelectric susceptibility

: the electric susceptibility. This is the electric twin of the magnetic story: plays the part of , and measures how easily the material polarises.

The local field

The field at the site of an atom is different from the macroscopic : it includes the fields of all the other polarised atoms, and in a dense solid they are close. It is built up in four pieces, :

, ,

in one lineThree mechanisms add up: the electron cloud shifts (, every atom), ions shift against each other (, ionic solids), permanent dipoles turn (, polar molecules). As the frequency rises they drop out one by one: dipolar first, then ionic, leaving the electronic part at optical frequencies.

Three ways to polarise

The total polarisability is the sum of whatever mechanisms the material allows:

wheretotal polarisabilityelectronic: electron cloud shifts against the nucleusionic: positive and negative ions shiftdipolar: permanent dipoles turn towards the field

Electronic polarisability

The electron cloud is displaced relative to the nucleus until the restoring pull of the nucleus balances the field. Model the cloud as a uniformly charged sphere of radius : the restoring force is linear in the displacement, like a spring, which gives , proportional to the atom's volume. The oscillator model adds the frequency:

At optical frequencies the polarisation is almost all electronic, and with (Maxwell): . This is how the refractive index measures .

Ionic polarisability

In an ionic crystal (NaCl, KCl) a field pushes the positive ions one way and the negative ions the other, stretching some bonds and compressing others. The bonds act as springs of stiffness , so each ion pair becomes a dipole with :

The ions are thousands of times heavier than electrons, so this mechanism resonates at much lower frequency (infrared, the lattice vibration frequency, Hz). It is comparable in size to : in NaCl it is about half the total.

Dipolar polarisability

Polar molecules (, HCl, ) have a permanent dipole moment . Without a field they point at random; a field turns them, thermal agitation resists, and the balance gives exactly the Langevin average of paramagnetism, with in place of :

Plot against : slope gives the dipole moment, intercept gives (the Debye method).

Frequency dependence

Each process has a relaxation time. When the field changes much faster than that, the process cannot follow and stops contributing. Dipolar orientation is slowest (whole molecules turning, drops out by microwave frequencies, – Hz), ionic next (infrared, Hz), electronic last (ultraviolet, Hz). So and fall in steps as the frequency rises. (A fourth, space-charge polarisation at interfaces, matters only at very low frequency.)

Near each step the material absorbs energy strongly (the dielectric loss peaks): this is why water absorbs microwaves and ionic crystals absorb in the infrared. Microwave ovens work at 2.45 GHz, where water's dipoles lag the field.

where marks get lost

Water's static but its refractive index is 1.33 (): the huge difference is the dipolar part, which is gone at optical frequencies. Never use unless both are at the same frequency.

Ferro- & piezoelectricity

in one lineA ferroelectric has spontaneous polarisation (the electric twin of ferromagnetism): a – hysteresis loop, a Curie point, and above it. A piezoelectric crystal (no centre of symmetry) polarises when squeezed, and strains in a field.

Ferroelectricity

Spontaneous polarisation: the centres of positive and negative charge do not coincide even with no field. Everything you learnt about ferromagnets carries over with for and for : domains, a – hysteresis loop (remanent polarisation, coercive field), and a transition temperature (Curie point) above which the crystal is paraelectric. Examples: barium titanate , Rochelle salt (), KDP.

Two groups:

  • Order–disorder: the transition is the ordering of individual ions, linked to protons in hydrogen bonds: (KDP), .
  • Displacive: a whole sublattice of one kind of ion shifts relative to another; perovskite and ilmenite structures: , , .

(perovskite): cubic cell above (about 393 K) with at the corners, at the face centres and at the body centre (octahedrally surrounded by six ); the charge centres coincide. Below , (and ) shift slightly up and down: the cell becomes tetragonal and polarised. The polarisation comes from induced electronic and ionic dipoles.

Why it happens: the polarisation catastrophe. From Clausius–Mossotti, diverges when reaches 1: the local field from the polarised neighbours alone is then enough to keep each ion polarised, so the polarisation sustains itself with no applied field.

Piezoelectricity

In some crystals a stress produces a dipole moment and so surface charges (direct effect); a field produces a strain (converse effect). Examples: quartz, Rochelle salt, tourmaline, and PZT ceramics.

In one-dimensional notation the two effects read:

wherepolarisationstresspiezoelectric strain constant (same in both equations)electric fieldpermittivity of free spacedielectric susceptibilitystrainelastic compliance

polarisation, stress, piezoelectric strain constant, field, dielectric susceptibility, strain, elastic compliance. The same constant appears in both equations: the direct and converse effects are two faces of one coupling. Large fields give small strains: in quartz V/m gives a strain of about .

learn this by heart

The ions must be displaced so that the charge distribution loses its symmetry: piezoelectricity needs a crystal with no centre of inversion (20 of the 32 point groups). Every ferroelectric is piezoelectric (), but not every piezoelectric is ferroelectric (quartz).

Uses: electromechanical transducers: pick-ups, microphones, strain gauges, ultrasonic generators, gas lighters, and quartz oscillators that keep time in every watch and computer.
